summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would make patients pay more for their medicines under two government schemes.
It does this by raising the amount patients must pay towards each prescription and the spending limits that trigger lower charges.
For concessional patients, the number of prescriptions needed to reach the lower-charge limit would rise by two each year from 2015 to 2018.
changes: Patient payments for each prescription would increase by 80 cents for concessional patients and $5.00 for general patients from 1 January 2015.
The spending threshold that lowers charges would rise by two prescriptions each year for concessional patients and by 10 per cent each year for general patients from 2015 to 2018.
These increases would be on top of the usual yearly price adjustment tied to the Consumer Price Index.
summary.affected: Patients who receive medicines subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme or the Repatriation Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Introduced the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, noting PBS costs have risen 80 per cent in a decade to around $9 billion a year, and proposed raising the general co-payment by $5 to fund a $20 billion Medical Research Future Fund expected to eventually provide $1 billion a year for research.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: Opposed the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2014, quoting former AMA vice-president Geoffrey Dobb's warning that the budget would set health care back more than 50 years, and noted the Howard government's 2005 pensioner co-payment rise from $3.70 to $4.60, a 24 per cent increase, saw use of some essential medicines fall by 11 per cent.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Supported the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, recounting the loss of his brother to type 2 diabetes, and cited PBS-subsidised drugs including insulin costing around $260 per prescription and a leukaemia drug costing $3,900 per script, with 24,572 prescriptions filled last year at a cost of $97 million to government.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, calling out the government's $55 billion in hospital funding cuts and a 13 per cent rise in PBS out-of-pocket costs, and mocked the Treasurer's comparison of the GP tax to the cost of a couple of beers when a trip to the doctor with two prescriptions and a blood test could cost nearly $100.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: Supported the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, noting Labor doubled the co-payment from $5 to $10 in 1985, and that since the coalition took office 181 new medicines have been listed on the PBS, including hepatitis C treatments costing $17½ thousand per course but only $6 for concession card holders.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Laming
speeches.brief: Supported the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, noting the coalition has already approved 131 new drug listings since taking office, and argued the $5 co-payment increase will have no effect on the more than half of PBS medicines that already cost less than the current co-payment amount.

speeches.speaker: Nick Champion
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, arguing it channels John Howard's 1987 description of Medicare as 'a total disaster' that he wanted to 'pull right apart', and accused the government of continuing efforts to dismantle universal health care.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Supported the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, projecting PBS costs will rise from $9.2 billion this year to $15 billion by 2023-24 and $30 billion within 20 years, and noted the government now pays $12 billion a year in debt interest, more than the entire PBS budget.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, calculating that his Blair electorate's 838,244 bulk-billed GP services last year would generate an extra $6.5 million in GP tax revenue, and said the West Moreton Hospital and Health Service would be $6.749 million worse off by 2017-18 under the government's funding changes.

speeches.speaker: Alannah MacTiernan
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, arguing that reforming generic drug pricing would save more than raising co-payments, citing analysis that Australia pays $514 million a year for the cholesterol drug atorvastatin compared with $119 million at English prices, and that only 35.4 per cent of Australian prescriptions by volume are generic compared with 84 per cent in the United States.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, and separately detailed how funding cuts forced the Royal Flying Doctor Service to withdraw from a mental health program serving 10 remote Aboriginal communities and more than 50 outstations west of Alice Springs, on top of $160 million in cuts to Indigenous health programs.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, contrasting the government's cuts to pensioners with its $22 billion Paid Parental Leave scheme, and recounted visiting the Tasmanian Pensioners Association, where members described elderly constituents considering giving up pets they could no longer afford to feed.

speeches.speaker: Julie Owens
speeches.brief: Opposed the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2014, which raises the general PBS co-payment by $5 to $42.70 and the concessional co-payment by 80 cents to $6.90 from 1 January 2015, arguing that cutting support for early health intervention will increase costs to taxpayers in the long run.

speeches.speaker: Bernie Ripoll
speeches.brief: Opposed the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2014 as a bad bill that will raise $1.3 billion over four years from sick Australians to fund a Medical Research Future Fund rather than the PBS itself, and cited senior doctors' warnings that the government's budget cuts would set Australia's health system back 50 years.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Opposed the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill 2014 as part of a $1.3 billion tax increase on medicines, contrasting it with the government's decision to let wealthy Australians earn more than $100,000 a year tax-free on superannuation balances of over $2 million.

speeches.speaker: Terri Butler
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill as part of a $1.3 billion tax increase on medicines, quoting health policy professor Stephen Duckett's warning that savings of over $1 billion a year would come off the backs of the poorest, and noted the United States spends nearly 18 per cent of GDP on health compared with about nine per cent in Australia.

speeches.speaker: Tim Watts
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, citing a COAG Reform Council finding that 36.4 per cent of Indigenous Australians already delay filling prescriptions due to cost, and warned the government will slash $1.8 billion from public hospitals including Williamstown, Sunshine and Western hospitals in his Melbourne electorate.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, warning it adds to $80 billion in cuts to public hospitals and schools, and said South Australia alone faces about $655 million in health funding cuts, equivalent to the cost of running Flinders Medical Centre.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Opposed the Pharmaceutical Benefits bill, noting the government's reluctance to debate it, and marked Medicare's 30th anniversary this year as a core achievement of universal health care that the bill's changes would undermine.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: Opposed the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill, citing a COAG Reform Council report finding 8.5 per cent of people delayed or skipped prescriptions due to cost, rising to 36.4 per cent among Indigenous people, and said the government's changes go beyond even the Commission of Audit's recommendations.

speeches.speaker: Anna Burke
speeches.brief: Opposed the National Health Amendment (Pharmaceutical Benefits) Bill as a $1.3 billion tax grab on medicines, saying the general co-payment would rise by $5 to $42.70, and cited a COAG report finding 36.4 per cent of Indigenous Australians delayed filling prescriptions due to cost.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Opposed the $1.3 billion tax increase on medicines, citing a COAG Reform Council report finding one in eight people in disadvantaged areas and more than one in three Indigenous Australians delayed or skipped filling prescriptions due to cost in 2012 to 2013.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: Opposed the $1.3 billion tax increase on medicines, saying her Lalor electorate accesses bulk-billing more than 1.5 million times a year and has 10,000 pensioners who would be hurt, and accused the government of hiding facts about Labor's own past PBS reforms.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Accused the coalition of gagging debate on the PBS bill after only four government MPs spoke on it, saying the changes would raise prescription costs by 13 per cent and increase the PBS safety net threshold by 10 per cent annually through to 2018.
